forces.title: Elevated UK Insolvencies Across Construction Sector
forces.description: UK construction continues to account for approximately 17% of all corporate insolvencies in England and Wales, with around 3,800 insolvencies over the past 12 months. Financial stress is spreading beyond SMEs and subcontractors to mid-sized and established firms, including main contractors, specialist subcontractors, fit-out businesses, and property services contractors. This poses a significant risk for debt recovery and credit assessment within the fixed income and insolvency resolution sector.

forces.title: Rising Interest Rates Increase Debt Costs for UK Businesses
forces.description: The Bank of England is expected to raise the Bank Rate to 4.00% by September 2026, with Gilt yields already at 4.80%. This makes refinancing and variable-rate debt materially more expensive for UK businesses, including those in machinery & equipment, which already face selective lending. This tightening of monetary conditions directly impacts the cost and accessibility of corporate debt, increasing financial pressure on borrowers and influencing lending standards.
forces.source_title: Q3 UK economic outlook: Growth holds, inflation bites

forces.title: Climate Protection Gap Amplifies Lending and Investment Risks
forces.description: A widening climate protection gap, where economic value is uninsured, directly propagates risks to lending markets. As insurance becomes unaffordable or unavailable, lenders tighten credit standards, shorten loan tenors, require more collateral, or increase interest rates. This can lead to broader pullbacks in lending, detrimental to economic activity and capital formation. The FSB explicitly recognizes this transmission channel, highlighting increased bank exposures in climate-vulnerable sectors and amplified financial stability risks in debt markets.
forces.source_title: Mind the protection gap: The risk to capital markets and the resilience financing imperative

forces.title: Climate Risk Integration Reshapes Debt and Equity Markets
forces.description: The increasing intensity and unpredictability of climate hazards are forcing financial markets to integrate physical climate risk into pricing and capital allocation decisions. This shift challenges traditional actuarial methods and valuation approaches, leading to higher premiums, tighter insurance terms, and reduced capacity. Consequently, debt and equity investors face increased costs, lower asset valuations, and constrained access to capital, fundamentally reshaping how risks are priced and transferred in fixed income and broader capital markets.
forces.source_title: Mind the protection gap: The risk to capital markets and the resilience financing imperative

forces.title: Private Credit Experiences Spread Compression and Borrower-Friendly Terms
forces.description: Intensifying competition from a growing capital base and re-sharpened bank/BSL market activity led to spread compression in global new-issue direct loans, falling to 544 basis points at year-end 2025 from 716 basis points in March 2023. Up-front fees also declined, and loan documentation became more borrower-friendly, with covenant-lite transactions rising to 21% of direct lending deals. These trends exert pressure on profitability for private credit lenders within the fixed income space.
forces.source_title: Private credit in 2025: A maturing industry navigates change

forces.title: Defaults and Liquidity Concerns Challenge Private Credit Stability
forces.description: The private credit industry is experiencing challenges, including a series of defaults and losses in leveraged credit. Public business development company (BDC) share prices traded significantly below net asset value (NAV) in 2025 and further in Q1 2026. Liquidity concerns emerged for many semi-liquid vehicles, with redemption requests nearly tripling in Q4 2025 and accelerating into Q1 2026, prompting some managers to limit fulfillment. These developments raise questions about credit quality and the interlinkages with the broader financial system.
forces.source_title: Private credit in 2025: A maturing industry navigates change

forces.title: Insurance Capital Fuels Private Credit Expansion Beyond Leveraged Lending
forces.description: Insurance and private credit are converging, driven by private credit's predictable yields and insurers' stable, long-duration capital. Goldman Sachs Asset Management's 2025 Global Insurance Survey revealed 58% of CIOs representing $14 trillion in assets plan to increase private credit allocations, particularly in investment-grade strategies and asset-backed finance (ABF). This structural alignment positions insurers as a key catalyst for private credit's ongoing expansion beyond traditional leveraged lending into a broader range of fixed income products.
forces.source_title: Private credit in 2025: A maturing industry navigates change

forces.title: LP Conviction in Private Credit Sustains Allocation Growth
forces.description: Institutional Limited Partner (LP) conviction in private credit remains firm, with 40% of LPs planning to increase allocations over the next 12 months, surpassing planned increases for private equity or real estate. This positive sentiment is driven by private credit's senior position in the capital structure, predictable income profile, and narrow return dispersion. This sustained investor appetite acts as a tailwind, supporting capital formation and growth within the private debt component of the fixed income market.
forces.source_title: Private credit in 2025: A maturing industry navigates change

forces.title: Recognizing Resilience Improves Financing Terms for Debt
forces.description: Financial institutions can reward active climate risk reduction by improving recognition of verified resilience measures in pricing and financing terms. This could include premium credits, deductible reductions, coverage enhancements, margin ratchets, covenant flexibility, or longer loan tenors where resilience materially reduces expected loss. By better capturing the value of avoided loss, accounting and reporting approaches can transform resilience investments from perceived costs into value protection, enhancing bankability and investability for debt-linked projects.
forces.source_title: Mind the protection gap: The risk to capital markets and the resilience financing imperative

forces.title: Slower Industrial Investment Constrains Machinery Sector Debt Demand
forces.description: Investment in machinery and equipment remains constrained as companies defer major projects due to economic uncertainty and tighter monetary conditions. Uneven global demand and rising commodity costs further add to pressure at a time of limited pricing power. Lenders are becoming more selective, impacting the availability and terms of corporate debt for the sector. This subdued industrial investment translates to weaker demand for new debt issuance from machinery and equipment companies, affecting the fixed income market.

forces.title: Highly Leveraged Retailers Face Increased Restructuring Risk
forces.description: UK retail continues to face pressure from weak consumer confidence and cost-of-living concerns, alongside rising operational costs. While stronger mid-market players show resilience, highly leveraged and private-equity-backed businesses are more exposed to restructuring risk. This vulnerability implies potential for increased corporate debt defaults, restructurings, and insolvencies within the retail segment, posing a key risk for creditors and practitioners in the fixed income and IBC sub-industry.

viewpoints.title: Widening Protection Gap Threatens Capital Markets and Economic Stability
viewpoints.description: The widening climate protection gap, where economic activity remains uninsured, poses a critical threat to capital formation and long-term growth. When insurance becomes more expensive or unavailable, its effects spread into lending, investment, asset valuations, and public finances, reducing overall bankability and investability. This is not merely an insurance issue but a fundamental challenge to the effective functioning of debt and equity markets, necessitating significant capital mobilisation for adaptation and resilience, a role the UK financial markets are well-placed to fulfill.
viewpoints.source_title: Mind the protection gap: The risk to capital markets and the resilience financing imperative

viewpoints.title: Private Credit Sector Maturing Amidst Intensifying Competition and Risks
viewpoints.description: The private credit asset class is maturing beyond simple leveraged corporate lending into a complex ecosystem, facing new cyclical and structural risks. While deal volumes held near historic highs in 2025, competition intensified, leading to tightening spreads and borrower-friendly terms. Increasing defaults, liquidity concerns in semi-liquid vehicles, and rising redemption requests in Q4 2025/Q1 2026 highlight a challenging performance environment. Success for managers will depend on precise capital deployment, disciplined underwriting, and proactive risk management in this evolving landscape.
viewpoints.source_title: Private credit in 2025: A maturing industry navigates change

viewpoints.title: Rising Bank Rate and Gilt Yields Increase UK Debt Refinancing Costs
viewpoints.description: The UK economic outlook anticipates a 25bps Bank Rate hike to 4.00% in September, with rates likely holding until H2 2027. This, coupled with Gilt yields at 4.80%, means refinancing and variable-rate debt for businesses and households will become materially more expensive. Proactive credit risk management is essential as insolvencies remain elevated across Western Europe, indicating a need for businesses to stress-test their rate exposure and budget for sticky inflation and higher borrowing costs.
viewpoints.source_title: Q3 UK economic outlook: Growth holds, inflation bites

Projected to drive $106 trillion in infrastructure investment over the next 14 years, creating significant capital needs for segments like infrastructure credit.
